subsubtopic: PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to call the attention of the House to a special ceremony which will take place on the lawns of Parliament this afternoon around 3.30, the unveiling of the statue of Lester B. Pearson, our former Prime Minister and the member of Parliament for Algoma East for some 20 years.
I hope every member of Parliament will be able to attend this special ceremony to honour the memory of a truly great Canadian who was the leader of a government with great vision, a government which gave us many of the social programs that we enjoy today, such as medicare, the Canada Pension Plan, and the Canada Assistance Plan. He also gave us our distinctive Canadian flag.
A choir from Central Avenue Public School in Elliot Lake, Ontario, under the direction of Lorraine Liss will
sing at this afternoon's ceremony. This choir is an appropriate part of this special occasion because Mr. Pearson, during his lifetime, was a great inspiration to tens of thousands of young Canadians as he represented us as a Secretary of State for External Affairs at the United Nations, as the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, as the Leader of the Opposition and finally as the Prime Minister of Canada from 1963 to 1968.
The legacy he left us as we entered our second century as a nation in 1968 was stronger, more compassionate and united nation after his many years of service to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the government is encouraging price gouging by drug companies at the expense of Canadians suffering from arthritis.
Lederle Cyanamid sells the same drug under two different names, Methotrexate and Rhumetrex. Methotrexate is sold to hospitals for 59 cents a tablet. Rhumetrex, the same drug, is sold to pharmacies for $2.32 a tablet.
This government knows consumers are being cheated but it is doing nothing about it. The Canadian Association of Rhumatologists voted last week to censure Lederle for this practice. Did the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs respond? Not a word, Mr. Speaker. The Conseil consultatif de pharmacologie du Quebec and the Ordre des pharmaciens du Quebec have both denounced this scam. I call on the consumer and corporate affairs committee to order the minister and this drug company to appear before it to explain this flagrant and repugnant pricing abuse.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government was re-elected in 1988 because Canadians recognized that we had a plan for economic renewal. We told Canadians that we would build on the successful foundation that we laid in our first term.

September 26, 1990
Canadians were aware of our program and gave us the mandate and legitimacy to proceed. And proceed we did.
We introduced UI reforms to improve the system and save $2 billion a year. We introduced a large corporation tax to ensure fairness and save another $2 billion a year. These bills have been in the Senate 205 and 173 days and counting. We introduced the goods and services tax to reform an archaic and decrepit system and improve the Canadian economy. We have acted on our pledge, yet at each turn, a foot dragging Senate is thwarting the legitimate and responsibly elected government. Obstructionism in the Senate is adding billions to the deficit. The Senate blatantly brags that it will kill the GST. Such contempt for a responsibly-elected government and its electors is astounding.
To quote Stephen Lewis, "Either we have a parliamentary democracy, or we don't". Reason must prevail. The people of Canada and their responsibly-elected government will not be so easily duped.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a ceremony later this afternoon the statue of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, Canada's only Nobel Peace Prize winning Prime Minister will be unveiled.
I would like to read a short excerpt from the second volume of his memoirs, and I quote:
My own experience has given me a great respect for those who discharge their political responsibility by working for the party of their choice, and especially for those who do so by serving, or seeking to serve, in Parliament or in other legislative bodies. There can be no prouder achievement than to be chosen by one's fellow citizens to speak and work for them in a freely elected assembly.
Those are values that all members of this House share, I am sure. It is a challenge for all of us to instil these values in all of the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, today we will honour the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson by unveiling a statue in his honour. A remarkable Canadian, Mr. Pearson's became well known for his peace initiatives and for promoting dialogue
between nations. So far, he is the only Prime Minister to have received the Nobel Peace Prize. Bravo, Mike!
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this summer Canadians learned much of blockades.
Throughout the summer months my riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin was no stranger to the native blockades that affected many of Canada's small towns. I am sure all members of the House agree that while many of the aboriginal demands are legitimate, the use of illegal blockades are not the means by which they are to be realized.
On a national scale, we have been witness to a small group of masked insurgents holding our justice system hostage, a group who do not represent the legitimate concerns or aspirations of the native people.
More insidious than this, down the hall from this very House, another blockade has been put in place, a blockade erected by a group of misguided Liberal senators. Being held hostage behind this blockade is the Canadian democratic parliamentary system that we know and enjoy.

Mr. Speaker, let us take a minute to look at the summer's events in agriculture.
A farm aid package to help boost disastrous farm incomes provided half measures. Over a billion was needed, but $500,000 came.
To meet current needs, another $1.25 billion for grain growers is needed now because of a drop in initial Canadian Wheat Board prices at prairie elevators of 22 per cent on August 1, and increases to the export subsidy program used by Europeans and Americans. The Americans are now over $55 U.S. a tonne and have effectively pushed the world price well below initial prices.
September 26, 1990

At the GATT, our government is negotiating Article XI. At issue is whether supply management for agriculture production can survive. The system eliminates wastage and overproduction, and assures consumers a secure supply of product in return for a fair price to producers.
Cabinet must direct our negotiators at GATT to reject the aggregate measure of support concept that assumes that when a marketing board's prices are above a so-called world price, then the difference be construed as a subsidy. We must strengthen Article XI and maintain the viability of our dairy, poultry and egg farms.

Mr. Speaker, last week Patricia Wong came to see me at my office in Bridgewater. She was eligible for the fee payer program of the Canadian Jobs Strategy and she was accepted into the cosmetology course at the Nova Scotia Community college.
But Patricia Wong and many like her have been disappointed and let down because the funding for that program has been cut off by the actions of the other place down the hall. The Government of Canada believes that the Patricia Wongs of this country deserve a fair break, and a reasonable chance.
I urge the Liberal leaders of the other place to give Patricia Wong and others like her their just due, and to respect the long standing principles of Canadian parliamentary democracy. Pass Bill C-21.
Either we have parliamentary democracy or we do not.

The Minister of Justice is hosting a meeting on Vancouver Island next month entitled "Women Towards the Millennium", the purpose of which is, according to the Minister, "to explore the position of women in Canadian society."
We do know that 60 women have been invited to this meeting, but who these women are remains a mystery. We also know that neither the Liberal or the NDP critics for the status of women have been put on the list.
Indeed, in speaking with representatives of national women's groups, I could find none who had been invited. Does it not seem unusual that such a meeting is being held without representation of the major women's groups in this country? Is it not equally unusual that not one female member of Parliament from this side of the House has been invited?
I think it is time for the minister to come clean with Canadian women and tell us what this meeting is really about, who is invited to it and why so many who work through their national organizations for gender equity are not on the minister's list.

Mr. Speaker, thousands of Canadians are angry, and rightly so. A group of Liberal senators, supported by Liberal Leader Jean Chretien, has betrayed them by ignoring the democratic choice they made by electing a majority government in 1988. Thousands of women are unable to take advantage of the benefits of Bill C-21, including maternity leave, because Liberal senators and Jean Chretien decided otherwise.
Thousands of unemployed workers have no hope of returning to work because Liberal senators and Jean Chretien are denying them the right to training. Thousands of Canadian men and women can no longer hope that reducing the deficit will put this country on the road to economic recovery because Jean Chretien and his senators have decided otherwise.
Canadians ought to know that the unwarranted action taken by the Liberal senators and Jean Chretien will increase the deficit by $8 billion.
Canadians ought to know that all our social programs and our economic future are being compromised by the unwarranted action of the Senate.

Mr. Speaker, Parliament has proven to be extremely poor in responding pro-actively

to environmental crises. The warning about zebra mussels fell on deaf ears and now the Great Lakes and its tributaries face contamination.
A few days ago Norwegian MPs appeared before Canada's environment committee and warned of the crisis facing Norway. Due to a major outbreak of parasitic disease, Norway has begun a program to kill all life in 70 rivers. Combined with the destructive effects of genetic pollution from salmon escaping from fish farms, Norway's wild salmon and rivers face extinction.
Let me quote the MPs from Norway, "This is maybe the main ecological problem in Norway, the most concrete we are facing" and "We cannot sit around tables debating while the salmon just die in the rivers." Further quotes are: "In the end the politicians gave in and the import occurred against the advice of the best informed scientists in the country" and "Some of the fish farmers went to Canada. They said we want bigger fish farms, we can do as we like."
Mr. Speaker, Norway is intentionally killing all life in 70 rivers. Failure to act here in Canada beginning today would be a crime. No Canadian river deserves a death warrant due to political negligence.

Mr. Speaker, in light of the forthcoming World Summit on Children, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House the plight of thousands of families across Canada who have suffered the disappearance of a child. It is our responsibility, as representatives of the people of Canada, to ensure that we offer protection and support to the victims and families of this crime.
We must support organizations such as the Missing Children's Network that works tirelessly for the protection of our youth.

Thanks to the perseverance of the Missing Children's Netword, dozens of children have been able to get back to their families. We must help organizations like these respond to the needs of those people in our communities who are confronted with the disappearance of a child.

Mr. Speaker, this morning we read in the papers that the Quebec Chamber of Commerce has rejected the constitutional status quo and wants the Quebec Government to ask Canada, in no uncertain terms, for all the powers it needs for its political, social and economic development.
This group of 60,000 business people feels Quebec has no choice. It must be able to act independently in the following areas: education, culture, communications, employment, manpower, unemployment insurance, regional development, financial institutions, health care, social and urban affairs, and recreation.
Mr. Jean Lambert, president of the Chamber of Commerce and former president of the "No" Committee in Quebec in 1980, made it clear these were minimum demands. I would advise the Mulroney government to reconsider the new approach it seems to have taken to Quebec as a result of pressures, namely from Ontario.
Taking a hard line will be useless. The Mulroney government's refusal to negotiate on a govemment-to-govemment basis with Quebec will merely stiffen the resolve of all Quebecers to get rid of a form of federalism that is no longer worthwhile.
The failure of the administrative agreement on immigration and Mrs. McDougall's announcement that she intends to create unilaterally a national occupational training commission, with no regard for Quebec's demands, and considering the failure to renew agreements.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to invite everyone in this House to participate in the unveiling ceremony of the Lester B. Pearson statue this afternoon.
September 26, 1990

As every member of this House will agree, this tribute is an occasion of honour and distinction. While the monument will remind us of Mr. Pearson's achievements, it should also serve to reinforce our responsibilities as parliamentarians. Mr. Pearson's conduct in the House serves as a model for us all. We should also take heed of his respect for parliamentary procedure, responsibility and tradition.
The current tactics undertaken by unelected senators with respect to passing government legislation would surely be frowned upon by Mr. Pearson. This monument, then, is not only an occasion of remembrance but it is also an echo from the past at a time when the integrity and responsibilities of the elected Parliament are hampered by the unaccountable Senate.
I know all Canadians will join with us in remembering and paying tribute to such a distinguished citizen and respected statesman. The thought, the emotion and the artistic energy expressed by the artist, will form a fitting tribute to the late Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson and we, as parliamentarians, can share with family, friends and colleagues in honouring "Mike" who contributed so greatly to Canada and Canada's stature in the world.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I would like every Canadian to ask themselves three questions.
One, should the unelected and unaccountable be the ultimate power in Canada over the elected and the accountable? Two, is this a desperate Senate action by Trudeau cronies to slow down the plunging popularity of Liberal Leader Jean Chretien, the shadow man? And thirdly, why has Jean Chretien consistently refused to state any alternative to the GST?
Again, all Canadians must reflect on the words of Stephen Lewis who is opposed to the GST but said: "Do we want a Parliamentary democracy or not?" The time to choose is now.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last night the Prime Minister said he would not hesitate to stack the Senate with eight additional Conservatives in order to ram through the goods and services tax.
Oh, oh.
Hear, hear.

The Prime Minister said this even though millions of Canadians have made representations to parliamentarians saying they do not want this unfair, regressive and damaging tax. In fact, Mr. Speaker, every measure of public opinion shows that the majority, the overwhelming majority of Canadians do not want this tax.
Instead of trying to stack the Senate, why will the Prime Minister not listen to Canadians for a change and scrap the GST?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend knows as well as I do that all tax measures tend to be unpopular and he indicates that public opinion is against the GST.
Public opinion is invariably against any new tax measure introduced by any government. But to run a government, looking out for the interests of the nation five, ten and twenty years from now, you cannot do so the way you run a hotline show and make fiscal policy based on the number of telephone calls you receive in the morning. We were elected with a mandate and we hope to have an opportunity to execute it.
I draw to my hon. friend's attention an editorial in one of Canada's leading newspapers, The Toronto Star, this morning. It stated:
In fact, Prime Minister Brian Mulroney won a parliamentary majority two years ago on a platform that included the GST-
Like a sepia-toned photograph of Liberal governments long dead, the lingering Liberal majority in the Upper House still has enough bodies and votes to defeat the tax. Regardless of the merits of the GST, or what happens to it, one thing is clear: Canadians need one government in Ottawa-not two.

September 26, 1990
Oral Questions
That is the parliamentary government. That is what we have and that is what-
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister is so interested in newspaper articles, why does he not look at the The Wall Street Journal that says: "Canada's Mulroney is leading the pack for title of the most unpopular leader of the western world"?
Oh, oh.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposed goods and services tax of the government is considered so unfair and damaging that three provincial governments, one of them a Conservative government, intend to challenge the GST itself in court, and intend to challenge the right of the Prime Minister to swamp the Senate with eight additional senators.
In 1981 when provinces went to court to challenge the way the then government was proceeding to amend the Constitution and bring it back to Canada, the government of the day withheld its activities and did not proceed until the court challenges were completed.
Why will the Prime Minister not follow this precedent and wait until the court challenges are decided before trying to stack the Senate with eight more GST-loving Tories?

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition has let the House in on a kind of an embarrassing secret that, in fact, I have become unpopular. I am embarrassed by that, but I am somewhat comforted by the view that so far my unpopularity lasts during the term but it changes quickly during an election campaign when the votes are counted.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the Right Hon. Prime Minister could answer the question.
Mr. Speaker, the last time they asked me to call an election they did not like the results.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps we could have another try.

All right, Mr. Speaker. In a final try, let me tell my hon. friends who are crying for an election that we are discussing the Constitution and one of the most important things I learned as a student of constitutional law is that a term in Canada is five years, not three.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that for two days in a row the Prime Minister insists he will not call an early election. He knows exactly the same thing that Canadians know, that whenever he calls an election he will not be there after that election.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again I ask the Prime Minister why he does not wait for the court rulings before appointing eight additional senators. Why does he not respect precedents, as previous governments did in the past. This is the same position as the one taken in 1981 by the Leader of the Opposition who is now his Secretary of State for External Affairs and who chose not to proceed until the courts had ruled?

What a joker, Mr. Speaker!
The Leader of the Opposition is urging us to respect precedents, yet his political allies in the Senate refuse to respect the most elementary precedent, namely that the members elected by the people must prevail over the non-elected senators.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. One province has already stated that it intends to challenge the federal government's right to act under Section 26 of the Constitution. One individual has already served notice that he is going to do so. Two other provinces may be challenging by this time next week. We are talking about the rights of the provinces here. We are talking about the rights of the people.
Oh, oh.

They do not believe in rights for anybody.

September 26, 1990

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member could put his question.
Mr. Speaker, 80 per cent of the people of Canada are opposed to the GST. We know he is not in favour of provincial rights and he is obviously not in favour of the opinion of Canadians-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member could hurry up and put his question.
Will the Prime Minister state categorically that he will wait until the court challenges are resolved before he appoints any additional Senators.
No.

Mr. Speaker, in a question that is this important and this unpopular to Canadians, Canadians have the right to hear the opinion of the courts. Why will the Prime Minister not respect this and wait for the court challenge to be answered?

Mr. Speaker, I think we have answered the questions very directly. It is quite surprising to see a veteran parliamentarian who has a good reputation in this place rising to suggest anything other than the supremacy of the elected members of Parliament over the rights of the Senate.
Mr. Speaker, it is wonderful to see the Liberals and the Tories fighting over the Senate. Neither of them did anything for 125 years to give us a legitimate Senate.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am tiying to assist hon. members to get on with Question Period. The hon. member will put his question as quickly as possible.

My question, Mr. Speaker, is directed to right hon. Prime Minister. Surely the Prime Minister realizes that he is on the brink of pushing the country into another constitutional crisis.
I want to ask the Prime Minister why he cannot see the wisdom of not causing a constitutional crisis in the name of an unpopular tax? Why not just withdraw the unpopular tax, save us from the crisis, and get about the business of real tax reform in the country?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to see the usually thoughtful member of the NDP make an argument that specious in regard to a role in Parliament that his party has consistently analysed in a different manner over the decades.
In fact, his hometown newspaper this morning provided some views that he ought to reflect upon. The Winnipeg Free Press stated that: "The Liberal majority's plan to kill the GST is a perversion of the useful role (of the Senate). It is a dangerous and irresponsible abuse of power which should concern all Canadians whatever they think of the GST". I assume that includes the NDP.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister will get nowhere with me quoting the Winnipeg Free Press. They were for the free trade agreement as well.
Does the Prime Minister not realize that we patriated the Constitution in 1982? What he is considering is a step which would put Canada back in a quasi-colonial status, having the Prime Minister go to the Queen in order to solve a Canadian political problem that he could solve by listening to the Canadian people and withdrawing the GST.
Call an election, Brian.

Oh, oh.
I have been trying to stay away from it, Jim.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, I never got an answer to my last question because it was taken over by this idle chatter between two representatives of the corporate elite in Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg-Transcona has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Prime Minister could answer the question as to why he wants to embarrass the whole country by going cap in hand to the Queen and, at the same time, explain why he continues to maintain that he had some kind of mandate for the GST when it was he and his colleagues who shut up the hon. member for Mississauga South when he mentioned the GST in the early stages of the 1988 campaign.

Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions, including November 17, 1988, October 1, 1988 and throughout, there were very specific and lengthy arguments by me in regard to our position on the GST. We said that if we were re-elected in 1988, if we received a mandate from the people of Canada in that election campaign, we would bring in and pass the GST. We have done that. That is the fundamental principle of democracy and I am astonished that a socialist will not stand up and acknowledge that.
My friend from Willowdale and I are being accused by the NDP of idle chatter between the corporate elite. Let me quote a spokesperson for the dispossessed and the downtrodden, Stephen Lewis, on the CBC yesterday morning. Mr. Lewis said: "And I must say that if Brian Mulroney were driven to the eight additional senators, I can't say I blame him. Ultimately, we have a parliamentary democracy and the way in which they are behaving in the Senate really drives me crazy".

Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Minister of Finance. The minister would know about the recent announcement that there have been at least 30,000 bankruptcies in Canada since the beginning of the year. Monetary policies, especially as they relate to overly high interest
rates, are strangling the Canadian economy. My question to the Minister of Finance is to find out whether at long last the government and the Minister of Finance acknowledge that they must change their monetary policy, let interest rates drop, and lower the value of the Canadian dollar?

Mr. Speaker, I should point out to the hon. member that while there are a significant number of bankruptcies, and I do not take any pleasure in seeing that, there have been something like 350,000 new businesses created in 1989. While there are companies that fail, there are considerably more companies that are being created because of the dynamic economy that we have had over the last six years.
Where?

The hon. member says, where. If he would care to look around in any part of this country, he would see that during this period of time we have had over 1.5 million jobs created. We have been one of the leading economies in the world. If the hon. member will not open his eyes to the progress that we have seen in this country over the last six years, there is no hope for him.
I say to my friend that over the past three months we have seen an alleviation in the implementation of monetary policy which resulted in a 1 per cent drop in the prime rate and about a 1.5 per cent drop in the Treasury Bill rate and the Bank of Canada rate. We are reflecting the change in the economic circumstances in the policies we have been following. If there is a continuation of the ease in inflation and of the ease in the economic conditions, that trend to lower interest rates can continue.

Mr. Speaker, the fact is that Canadian business cannot wait. The high interest rate policy is driving thousands of them out of business. If he looks at the job creation he is referring to, he should realize that we are losing jobs in the manufacturing and exporting sector.
Does the Minister of Finance understand that this is just the tip of the iceberg? If he is listening to business in this country, he should realize that the last nail in the coffin of the Canadian economy is going to be the goods

and services tax if it passes. Is the minister going to wake up to the economic realities in this country or not?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's question would have some legitimacy if he had an alternative to the goods and services tax. His colleague from Ottawa said that the credibility of the Liberal Party would be in shreds if the Liberal Party of Canada, through its non-elected Senate, votes down the GST when it does not have an alternative to put in place.
If the hon. member is concerned about the business community in this country, he will listen to what the business community is saying about the tactics of the Senate. The people in the business community are saying that if the GST is stopped now by the unelected Senate, there will be chaos in the business community. If the hon. member does not want to see that sort of thing happen, he should speak to the people in the Senate and tell them to get on it and pass this legislation in the interest of the people that he is concerned about.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of National Revenue and it is simply this: Will the Minister confirm for the House today that he has instructed businesses across Canada to begin advance collection of the goods and services tax even though it is not the law of Canada?

answer, Mr. Speaker, is no. If the hon. member would welcome the invitation that I gave him for a briefing, I would be very happy to let him know the rules of C-62.

collected until both Houses of this Parliament pass the law?

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister.
In his announcement to the House of Commons yesterday, the Prime Minister appeared to make an offer in good faith to the aboriginal people. Yet, yesterday again, the Liberal premier of Quebec rejected a modest three point proposal which would have allowed an honourable disengagement at Oka rather than the humiliating defeat which Premier Bourassa seems to be committed to.
Is the Prime Minister prepared today to facilitate an honourable disengagement at Oka and to finally settle this dispute in good faith in accordance with the gesture he made yesterday?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister did indeed make a wonderful speech to this House yesterday along with a number of very, very positive undertakings to the aboriginal people of Canada. All Canadians can be justly proud of the record of this government, which we will continue and supplement on behalf of our aboriginal people.
In fact, when the warriors in the treatment centre put down their arms and come out, we will be able to make great progress on behalf of the aboriginal people of Canada.

Hear, hear.

Oral Questions

A supplementary. The Prime Minister promised to reconsider his government's comprehensive claims policy which most people acknowledge as a key factor in the Mohawk's grievance. Will he take the advice of the Coolican report and the Canadian Bar Association and recognize aboriginal title in a new claims policy? Will he introduce legislation to create an independent aboriginal claims commission? What is the Prime Minister prepared to do to prove his offers were made in good faith and are not yet another set of empty promises to aboriginal people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the record of achievement of this government on behalf of aboriginal people is far and away more generous and has advanced the cause of aboriginal people far more than any previous government in the history of this country. We appreciate the discussions, the important contributions made yesterday and by aboriginal leaders. We will continue to develop these programs in consultation with aboriginal people.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister of Canada with regard to his broad, sweeping statements made yesterday to accelerate the comprehensive land claims process.
No specific commitment to changing the outdated claims policy, which is very divisive, was made. This is viewed as being another empty promise. The extinguishment policy which I referred to violates the fiduciary responsibility the government has for aboriginal peoples.
I ask the Prime Minister, will he make a commitment here and now to abolish this destructive extinguishment clause in the comprehensive land claims policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know how deeply the hon. member is concerned about the cause of aboriginal people and the nature of the comprehensive claims policy. We will have ample opportunity to further the discussions which were held in this House these past 24 hours with members of the various caucuses and parties. I will be personally examining many of the fine contributions that were made here in these important debates.

Mr. Speaker, since I have not received an answer to my question, I redirect this question to the Prime Minister. My supplementary is to the Prime Minister.
If he does want to reintroduce the dignity and trust he spoke of into the process of consultation and negotiation of such items as comprehensive land claims, will he commit to this House and aboriginal groups to changing the outdated land claims policy by accommodating the Penner and Coolican reports on the abolishment of the extinguishment policy here and now today. Yes or no.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was present in the House, as was the hon. member, when the Prime Minister indicated that one of our most significant priorities would be to deal with the claims process in terms of specific claims, in terms of the treaty land entitlements which have not been fulfilled and in terms of changes to the comprehensive claims policy which would allow us to expedite the processing of these claims.
I ask the hon. member to show some trust and confidence that we will be able to make these changes, as the Prime Minister has promised.

In the absence of the Minister of Immigration, Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Minister of State for Employment and Immigration and Minister of State for Seniors.
Figures indicate that federal funds for teaching French to immigrants have decreased by 17 per cent in the last year while the number of immigrants has gone up by 12 per cent during the same time.
Mr. Speaker, some immigrants have to wait up to five months before being able to register for French lessons. Can the minister explain why the government cannot make this program more readily accessible to immigrants who need to learn French to make their transition into their chosen society that much easier?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for this question

which enables us to stress again that the government does give priority to immigrant linguistic training.
This is why in excess of $120 million was earmarked for language training in 1990-91, three times as much as in the 1984-85 budget. Still I hasten to point out to my colleague opposite that budgets and programs have to be re-examined every year. We do that in close co-operation with our provincial colleagues to make sure that our programs are indeed tailored to real needs.

Mr. Speaker, only a few days ago, the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council said in recommendation No. 7 that the Council recommended making French-language training available to all immigrants in Quebec. This morning, the Quebec Department of Immigration confirmed the information we got from the media, namely that there had been a reduction of 17 per cent. Why doesn't the government listen to its own advisory council and immediately increase funding to make French-language courses for immigrants available to all?

Speaking on behalf of this government, I am very much aware of the importance of making this kind of training available to immigrants. I want to repeat that $120 million have been earmarked within our budget. We want to manage our programs effectively, and I can inform the House that the programs approved this year are three times what they were in 1984-85. That is quite an improvement.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence. The ongoing situation in the gulf, which is dangerous and serious, continues to concern Canadians and the people of the world.
Oral Questions
There are authoritative reports that the U.S. intends to launch an offensive attack on Iraq completely outside the terms of the United Nations resolution.
Will the minister instruct the Canadian contingent in the gulf that it is strictly to limit its activities to those which are within the terms of the UN resolution and that under no circumstances is it to become involved in precipitated U.S. offensive action against Iraq?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is right in assuming that there is a serious international crisis in the gulf. I suggest he is foolhardy in relying on his information through the newspapers as to reports of actions taken by governments.
That being said, I can assure him that before any changes are made to the mission that Canadian forces are involved in at this time in support of the United Nations sanctions, resolution 665, that of deterring aggression, they will have to be consulted and we will have to make that change in Canada. It will not be changed by the commanders in the area.

Mr. Speaker, among the sources for the suggestion that there is an offensive U.S. policy is none other than the recently fired chief of the air force in the United States of America. This has been supported by all kinds of independent analysts.
I would like to know and this House would like to know what steps the Government of Canada is taking to persuade the United States to give sanctions and the United Nations a chance to get the hostages free and to get Iraq out of Kuwait.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):

Let me go a little further and suggest to the hon. member that the actions taken by the ambassador of Canada and United Nations Ambassador Fortier since the outset have been to convince all nations involved to abide by the United Nations resolutions. Canada has co-sponsored on several occasions those resolutions.

September 26, 1990

Canada has been working consistently since the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq to bring about a peaceful resolution through the United Nations.
I suggest to the hon. member that what he sees taking place, the enforcement of the resolutions by the world and that world condemnation, is proof that Canada and other countries including the United States are prepared at this time to work through the United Nations.

Last spring this government took away interest-free cash advances from farmers. That was a horrible mistake, and it hurt farmers.

One of the goals of the summit will be to plan a concerted attack on world poverty among children. One of the commitments of this government is to continue to do everything that we can to reduce the rate of poverty among children.
I am pleased to be able to tell the hon. member that since 1984 we have been able to reduce by over a quarter of a million, the number of children who are living under the low income cutoffs. We are determined to continue to keep that effort and do everything that we can to reduce the level even further.

Mr. Speaker, very sadly, there are at least one million Canadian children who are poor and dying. We cannot long endure their continued loss to ignorance, abuse, and ill health. September 26, 1990

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member raises a very good point. It is a very serious one as far as the government is concerned.
He is right. We have harvested a better than average crop. It has come off in good condition. We find totally unacceptable the bill that was passed in the U.S. Senate about 10 days ago, targeting specifically Canadian markets.
We are examining very thoroughly and very carefully the possibilities of pursuing an action under the free trade agreement. Once that advice is complete, we will then be in a position to make a decision.
In the meantime we are making strong representations to the U.S. administration to not see that the bill comes into law because, if it does come into law, there are some very pertinent implications as far as the free trade agreement is concerned that we intend to pursue.

Mr. Speaker my question is also for the Minister of Agriculture. Both dairy and poultry producers across Canada are concerned about the future of supply managed commodity sectors and therefore the future of the Canadian product that is produced by those farmers.
When the Canadian position on agriculture is tabled at GATT on or before October 15, can we have the minister's assurance that the supply management programs will not be jeopardized but will be strengthened by better support in Article XI of GATT and further, that they will not be compromised by any Canadian support for the aggregate measure of support formula?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure my hon. colleague knows that the balanced position Canada has developed with respect to our position at the GATT negotiations has
been brought about as a result of extensive consultations with the provincial governments and with all sectors of the agricultural industry. I think it is fair to say that there is general approval for the position that Canada has taken.
We have proposed the strengthening and clarification of Article XI and have outlined the manner in which that will be done. The position we have taken is that we are asking all participating countries to reduce trade distorting levels of support in all three areas. We consider that the aggregate measure of support is a useful tool in terms of monitoring the level of that support. What we are proposing are really reductions that would be considered to be direct support by the government. Of course that would all be conditional upon the other participating countries taking similar action.

Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege is partly related to something that happened yesterday in the Legislative Committee on Bill C-79, the Parliament of Canada Act. You must have noticed the problem since you testified before the Committee.
Briefly, the list of committee members shows me as a member of the Progressive Conservative Party, although everyone knows that since May 18,1 have had no further interest, either directly or indirectly, in the party and no longer wish to be associated with it.
It goes further than that, however. It seems that despite my speech in the House on May 18, 1990, my name continues to be associated with the Progressive Conservative Party in various committees, and I make this statement today, Mr. Speaker, to ensure I am no longer associated with this party, either in committee or in any other way.
Furthermore, although nearly 3 per cent of the people in Laurier-Sainte-Marie do not agree with me, 68 per cent will probably appreciate my position.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to get to the main problem which affects my privileges in this House and indeed one of the rights recognized by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and I am referring to freedom of association. I would like to read the following-for the benefit of those who might be watching at home, these glasses belong to my friend, Mr. Plamon-don-and I quote: "The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantees the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law
as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society."
Everyone has the following basic freedoms: freedom of conscience and religion, of course, but also freedom of association.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege was twofold.
You have dealt with the first part regarding my former affiliation with the Progressive Conservative Party. The second part has to do with my name being mentioned in official documents of the House and especially on air when the proceedings are broadcasted, as it is the case now.
I request, in the name of the freedom of association and pursuant to the Charter of Rights, the right of freedom of association, that fundamental right I had to be associated with my colleagues of the "Bloc Quebecois". I also request that the Canadian people, as well as the people of Quebec and of my riding of Megantic-Compton-Standstead, be informed of my new political allegeance, the political affiliation I have chosen under the Charter of Rights and in accordance with the basic principles of democracy in our society.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that precedents on this subject dating back in many instances 200 or 300 years cannot be put forward, given that the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms takes precedence over any other text or privilege since coming into effect in 1981.
Your ruling will have to be based exclusively on the Charter, setting aside precedents from another era.
This alliance, as you have been officially advised, was agreed to and signed by the new members of a group called "Bloc Quebecois", and must be recognized as such. In fact, what would it mean to recognize the right of association, the freedom of assocation, if you were not to recognize this group and call it by its name. You cannot simply say: You, the member for Megantic-

Compton-Stanstead, are entitled to associate with the member for Richelieu, as long as it is kept under wraps.
On this matter, I don't think you can afford to bury your head in the sand. My request, Mr. Speaker, is supported by the most fundamental texts in our country, which are widely recognized in every nation of the world and by all governments and democratic assemblies.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, in the Committee on the Review of the Parliament of Canada Act, we had practically the same discussion, not exactly the same but almost.

I think it is clear from our precedents in this Parliament, let alone previous Parliaments, that it is the right of members in terms of designation to remove the designation they had when they arrived in this place. If they ran under the Canada Elections Act under a particular party name and they choose no longer to be a part of that, then that is their choice. I discovered through conversations some months ago that no one else can take the designation away from them. That is a matter of individual choice and is well centred in our parliamentary democracy.
The issue the member is raising dearly today is whether or not he has the right to substitute for that designation a new designation of some kind. I am not sure; perhaps it would take a bit of table research to decide whether or not we really have any kind of clear precedents for the power to put a different set of words behind one's name in all of our publications including Hansard.

On the issue related to the Board of Internal Economy, it has not met since that correspondence arrived. It would probably be premature to send any of the other matters to committee at this point.

September 26, 1990
Speaker's Ruling

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we accept the proposal by the Government Whip that this question be referred to a Standing Committee of the House for examination and consideration, with the recommendation to act with the requisite diligence so that this matter can be settled as soon as possible.
There is a problem. Two more issues were raised by the hon. member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead in his statement. On television we see the member's name, and if I am not mistaken, some indication of the political party to which he belongs. I think we have to say, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very important matter that concerns all members of this House, and I think we will have to determine whether independent groups of members constitute a political party in this House and whether we should refer to them as members of a political party, a political affiliation, a group, a coalition or a block.
That, in fact, is another matter, of some concern to us, and I simply want to inform the independant member for Megantic-Compton-Stanstead who spoke earlier that here again we feel that the entire question could be referred to a committee of the House for discussion. We are willing to discuss the matter here in the House, but it is not that easy. In fact, it is a very complex matter. To some observers, it may seem trivial, but for us the designation of a political party, a block, a group, a
coalition or what have you is essentially a matter regarding the organization of this House. Mr. Speaker, we know the British tradition, even in the way the seats are assigned, with the government on your right and the opposition on your left, suggests the existence of a long standing tradition where there is a government and an opposition, and the fact that the latter is divided into parties, groups or simply composed of independant individuals is not important.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a comment or two about the two amendments, motions No. 1 and No. 2, which were grouped for debate. They are technical amendments relating to wording changes that were not caught at the time of the committee hearings. I will speak more on third reading.
These two amendments are very much in the tradition and nature of the spirit that characterized the work on Hibernia. As we enter this last phase on the debate on Hibernia, it is important for the House to know what actually happened in respect of this long-awaited project. What took place was simply this.
It goes back to the mid-1960s when the then Premier of Newfoundland, the Hon. Joey Smallwood, in an act in the best traditions of Newfoundland politics, decided to hire a boat and crew to go to the Grand Banks and used deep-sea divers to place on the floor of the ocean a plaque designating that the resources that some day would be discovered on the Grand Banks. He obviously had visions which others at that time might not have shared. With the placing of that plaque on the floor of the ocean, he claimed those resources for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador.
It was no different, I would suggest, than that which we on the Prairies faced at the time when we entered Confederation and were not seen wither worthy or capable of ownership of resources. In fact, the three prairie provinces did not get ownership to their resources-Manitoba, when it entered Confederation in 1870,
September 26, 1990

and Saskatchewan and Alberta in 1905-until the passage in the House of the Natural Resources Transfer Act of 1930.
In respect of Newfoundland and Labrador, I will not go through a lot of history today. My colleagues from that province on both sides of the House know the history of their province much better than I do, but this summer particularly I have been somewhat steeped in the history and folklore of those people and their province.
With the Atlantic Accord came the dream that Joey Smallwood and, I am sure, many Newfoundlanders and Labradoreans had-the dream that those resources would in fact been seen by the rest of Canada as being a resource, in this case, equally shared between Canada, in the right of Canada, and the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. It is that spirit which has surrounded this bill as it has made its way through the House and its committees.
In the committee, there were quite a number of amendments and members of both sides of the House were very co-operative and I want to thank them for that again. They were co-operative because as we were moving this enabling legislation through the House and the committee, we were also negotiating in Toronto. Therefore I had to make amendments as the negotiations were going on. Generally in this place, as most members with any experience know, it is very difficult to get legislation passed or amendments passed until every t is crossed and every i is dotted in the contractual form. That was the spirit in which this committee worked. These are the two amendments that were not caught that evening and it is in that same spirit that these amendments are brought forward.
At this time, as we enter report stage, it is important to understand what happened in Newfoundland. When the announcement on Hibernia was finally made, obviously the people of Newfoundland and Labrador welcomed this development. I was honoured to be there along with my colleagues and I invited all members of the House to that event. I was there with my colleague, the Minister for International Trade who is the hon member for St. John's East. I have had words with other colleagues from
Government Orders
the other side of the House with respect to what happened that day.
It is important for us to know that for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, while the Hibernia project will not bring the kind of wealth or possibly the bonanza that some have always hoped for, that it was seen, as the Prime Minister said, as more than simply another deal. It is more than barrels of oil or economic activity. Rather, it is an issue relating to fairness, equity, and dignity.
I hope that this legislation is seen in that light and, while it benefits the people of Newfoundland and Labrador in the first instance as it should, that members on both sides of the House will recognize that it brings the final act in legislative and legal terms to fruition.
I also hope that members of the House from other provinces will recognize why it is important, first, for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador. They do not want to be recipients of equalization any more than any other province, but rather want to contribute to the financial well being of Canada as they have always wanted to do. So, we must look at this bill as having benefits in the first instance for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, but also as having great benefits for the residents of other provinces of Canada. I have never known major projects that can ever be isolated or insulated for benefits to only one province or region.
I am reminded of years ago when I was Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and it seems like years ago, in 1979. I was on a drilling rig in the Beaufort Sea. On the drill floor I met a fellow who must have been at least 135 pounds dripping wet. I asked him where he was from and he said: "From Newfoundland." I said: "Well, what are you doing here?" He answered: "Well, it is pretty obvious. I am drilling for oil."
I always thought of that when I heard people say that the people from Newfoundland would not get benefits out of this project because they do not have either the expertise or the experience. It was my understanding and my knowledge that they had been willing to go to all comers of the world to work on projects such as these. I asked him why he was there and he said: "So I can earn some money to go back home, build a house and get

September 26, 1990
Government Orders
married." I thought that was a fairly legitimate objective as well.
I use that human story to point out that in this place we can very often get tied up with all kinds of legal arguments and political games. Let us remember that this legislation is good, first for the people of Newfoundland and Labrador, and also for all of Canada.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. I will then recognize an NDP member and then the hon. member for Richelieu.

Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to say how honoured and privileged I am to rise, both as the member from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception on the east coast of Newfoundland and as the associate critic for energy, mines and resources, to speak to these amendments.
As the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said, this is very much a housekeeping amendment and as such I have no detailed comments per se. If I could be permitted, there are a number of comments I would like to make at this point in time.
I would like to say at the outset that, as a Newfoundlander, I am very pleased-in fact, I am overwhelmed- about what this is going to do. Again, as the Minister said, this is not the be all and an end all. There are all kinds of i's to be dotted and t's to be crossed. But I would like to make the point that it is good not just for Newfoundland, it is good for all of Canada. The expenditures that are going to be involved and the oil resources and revenues are going to benefit Canada, not just from the participation and the spinoffs economically, but, indeed, reducing our dependence on white oil.
If I can perhaps be allowed a bit of a motion in this particular aspect, I would again look at the Newfoundland benefit. I would like to go back to the reference the hon. Minister made with respect to the Hon. J.R. Smallwood, the first Premier of Newfoundland. Indeed, it is generally well known by anybody who has been involved with Hibernia that he was the first. He sent a diver down on the Grand Banks because he believed in his province and he believed that if we were going to
succeed as a province in the long run we were going to have to diversify from the 1497 comment of John Cabot who said: "Fish were teaming. You can catch them in baskets." It is not quite that way any more.
At about the time that Mr. Smallwood was laying the plaque at the bottom of the Grand Banks, I was a lot younger than I am now. I remember the kind of songs that we used to sing in folklore, songs like Lots of Fish in Bonavis Harbour, Lots of Fishing Around Here; songs like Tickle Cove Pond; songs like The Trinity Cake; songs like A Great Big Sea Hove in Long Beach. Happy songs. Songs that said that although there were always hardships in Newfoundland we could always see through the hardships because there was always the hope that something would come along next year. I remember my grandfather having tough years and good years in the fishing and his father before him. There was always hope that something would come along that we did not have to have these alternatively good and bad years.
Now what are we seeing in Newfoundland just before Hibernia was signed again? The song that is now being sung and understood very much in Newfoundland, if I could be permitted, is a song made popular by the late Stan Rogers, a very well known folk singer. It is a very emotional song. I do not propose to sing it for you, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to give you the chorus. The song is called Make and Break Harbour and the chorus is a very sad chorus and it goes like this:
In Make and Break Harbour the boats are so few
Too many are hauled up and rotten
Most houses stand empty
Old nets hung to dry are blown away, lost or forgotten.
Forgotten, Mr. Speaker, because of the state of the economy dependent on the fishery almost as a sole industry. Yes, we have forestry and pulp and paper, but fishery is our mainstay.
In Newfoundland in the last two years-and I do not mean to be political about this but I have to take it from my end and portray at least the 100,000 constituents in Bonavista-Trinity-Conception-you have got goods and services tax, you have claw-back, you have got Bill C-21, you have got a reduced, total allowable catch, and you have got foreign overfishing. Wherever you turn around when you get up in the morning, life is not good.

Hibernia represents perhaps a change from the "Make and Break Harbour" syndrome and perhaps a change from the no-hope syndrome that so many of my people report to me and that I have witnessed myself.
Apart from the discussions that will take place here tonight, apart from the housekeeping amendments, apart from all the things that will go on, the one thing that it has given Newfoundland is hope, hope in the midst of despair, hope still for the ocean, but hope in a different aspect, in a different dimension of the ocean.
Mr. Speaker, I wish you could have been in St. John's, Newfoundland on September 14, a week ago Friday. I know the hon. Minister was there. The feeling is very difficult to translate. It did not matter which party you were from. It did not matter what part of Newfoundland you were from. It did not matter whether you had an invitation or not.
The almost 1,400 people who attended that reception in the Hotel Newfoundland was something to behold. The whole thread of hope went right through that reception. That emotion is still with us in Newfoundland. We know that there is more to it than this and we know the spin-offs are not just for Newfoundland. They are for the rest of Canada and we are happy about that. We in Newfoundland are not greedy. We are very pleased to be able to share a project of this nature.
I would be less than total and complete in my introductory comments if I did not admit that the majority of this project, that is the building of the gravity base structure will take place almost in the epicentre of my riding, near Sunnyside, about four miles from it at Mosquito Cove near Bull Arm, nice picturesque words. There is hope.
There is one other comment I would like to make. I have not been in this political business very long, but I have been involved in different aspects of different bills. I must say that it gave me, as a neophyte politician, great hope in the politics and in the business of doing these kind of things in this House, the highest court in the land, when I saw the kind of co-operation we received in getting this bill through. I believe we started first
Government Orders
reading, if my memory serves me correctly, on November 7 last year. We had another round I believe on February 9 for second reading. We got through committee stage shortly after, I think about June 6 or 7.1 remember the hon. minister and his staff making themselves immediately available. It was detailed, it was hard work. We worked into the night and we finished it very quickly and very amicably.
I would also say that I am very conscious, as I know my Newfoundland colleagues are, and I hope the House is very conscious of the personal hard work and energy the the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources put into this. I am sure the hon. Minister of International Trade and others did also. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: What has this got to do with Newfoundland?

I am sure the member from Newfoundland who was so active in the constitutional debate, in his heart of hearts being a red Tory, would not favour the privatization of Petro-Canada.
I am sure he would recall that the public institution was formed back in 1974-75 because of an OPEC crisis in the world and the escalating oil prices and because we had a minority parliament where the NDP insisted that we have this public co-operation which would be a window on the oil industry in this country. That is why we had Petro-Canada.
It strikes me as ironic that at the time when there is another crisis in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf this government would want to privatize Petro-Canada. I think it is very important that we mention that in this debate on Hibernia.
We have to deal with these amendments before the House, Mr. Speaker. It is very important that we mention that at this particular time because the people of this country must be made aware of the ideological blinders on the government across the way.
It is like the province of Saskatchewan where the premier a year or so ago tried to privatize the Saskatchewan Energy Corporation and the opposition New Democratic Party walked out of the legislature and let the bells ring. The people of that province, my province, rebelled and forced the government to withdraw the bill to privatize the energy corporation of Saskatchewan.
Mr. Speaker, I perhaps want to give you advance warning that when the privatization bill for Petro-Canada is tabled in this House in a few days, we intend to make that a fight across this country and show the people
September 26, 1990

of this country what the Conservative party is planning to do with their money.
The people of Canada do not agree with the Conservative Party of Canada. Come the election campaign in 1992-93 the Conservative Party will go down to a very resounding defeat.
It is short-sighted to embark on some of these policies. It is very short-sighted. We are running out of resources in this country. Under the free trade agreement we will be exporting more and more gas and oil to the United States, and it seems to me very unwise that they have moved to privatize Petro-Canada. I raise that at this time in the Hibernia debate because this is only part of the energy policy of the Conservative Party. What they have done here is they have signed a sweetheart deal that will benefit in the main some of their wealthy friends in the oil industry. I just wonder whether it will be of great benefit to the people of Newfoundland. How many jobs will this create in Newfoundland? How many long-term jobs in Newfoundland will this create? I see many of these megaprojects that cost millions of dollars for the creation of one good long-term job, millions and millions of dollars. If it would create a lot of jobs for unionized workers, I would be very happy and very surprised, but I am sure that will not be the case.
When we discuss these amendments, I hope the Conservative Party across the way will look very seriously at amendments that we are proposing and we are moving which will demand more accountability. Do you know that under this deal right

September 26, 1990

now, not one petrochemical plant industry can be built in Newfoundland from the offshore petroleum resources until existing industrial capacity is satisfied in three other provinces in Canada under an agreement between the Province of Newfoundland, under the former government, not the present government and this government in legislation passed before this House.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address some remarks on this motion as well. I just want to answer the question asked by the hon. member from Newfoundland. He asked where all their energy resources had gone. Under the previous Liberal government, the Trudeau government, they all went to the federal government and at least the Conservatives have split it fifty-fifty, between the provinces and the feds in terms of control and so on. -and as my colleague points out, they will lose equalization payments in return. Let us be careful of who is benefiting from this.

Oh, oh!

It is not fair. I say that and I am from British Columbia. It is not fair. It is part of the reason for bad blood between Newfoundland and Quebec. We are going to have to create some good blood and one way is to renegotiate that deal. I can say that because I am an outsider to this but I know a little bit about it. Second-

Hear, hear.
September 26, 1990

Not so fast! Wait until I finish. Provided the platforms are built by Canadian, not Quebec but Canadian companies. If Quebec is not in the Canadian Confederation: no jobs, nothing, no Canadian companies in Quebec.

So if they leave, they do not get any jobs at all. They are gone. This is entreprises canadiennes. Some of them may be in Quebec-

I want to see Quebec.
United.

No, but Quebec in Confederation with Canada.

Perhaps there will be a new relationship but in here. You know, if Quebec leaves, I tell my friends, there will not be any jobs. I tell the member from Hull none of his constituents will be working over here, my friend, so perhaps he had better deal with that.
But, Mr. Speaker, the real issue is perhaps highlighted by what the Minister of Energy told the committee. Hibernia is a big, fat subsidy to the multinational oil companies. We have given our major oil find to Mobil Oil and its friends. It is unbelievable. We are guaranteeing $1.7 billion in loans and we are giving a grant of $1 billion. That comes to $2.7 billion for the oil companies, the very companies that say, "Let's go by the market". Nice market, eh, if you can have it subsidized by the Canadian government and have it guaranteed by the Canadian government. That is a free market? Well, that is rather a different definition of the free market.
Here is the minister in front of the committee. The NDP member for Edmonton East asked him:
What is the department's best estimate of the percentage of Hibernia production that will be shipped to foreign market and never seen in a Canadian refinery?
In other words, are they going to refine it here. I asked the minister to respond to this in the House. He said in committee:
Mr. Chairman, it is possible that some of the production over a given period of time entirely could go to a refinery other than Canadian-

My friends, this means not Quebec or Newfoundland, but New York and New Jersey-

-where the home companies are.
The minister continues:
- primarily refineries in the northeast United States. It will depend quite frankly on Canadian refineries bidding on the sum of that crude.
We have to bid for it and we have to depend on Mobil and Exxon. Do you know where they are going to send it? They are going to send it to their own. We will not be coming by chance. There are no chances in this one. They will go to the parent.
Hibernia represents practically the greatest giveaway in the century of Canadian resources. The reason is that Mobil and the oil companies have control. Petro-Canada should have been running that entire operation or some other Canadian company should be running it.
When I sat on the energy committee as NDP energy critic for eight years and went up and down the national energy program, we studied a thing called sourcing. It was Bill C-48 in those days. We had witnesses from all over the world: from Norway, the United Kingdom and other countries that were involved the North Sea. We learned that you have to target your sourcing. You have got to require sourcing.
That is why it is a good amendment for Canadian companies-and I say it again.

We should get some of those. We have to guarantee that some of those platforms will go to Quebec, that all the oil will be refined in Canada, and that the benefits will go to other parts of the maritimes and spread out into Ontario and the rest of the country. It just does not happen because Hibernia is going to be run by Mobil and the other companies. There is the minister's own testimony. The government is guaranteeing the project and giving vast loans. It wants to tackle the deficit. What a giveaway that is. Then it bribes the people.

Government Orders
The people of Newfoundland are poor. They need jobs and they need aid from the federal government. They say: "There is a billion dollars". It is balderdash. "It is a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. Don't really diversify your economy, Newfoundland; just get this big megaproject and you will be all right".
This is all very well now when the price of oil is going up, but if the price of oil goes down-I predict below $40 Canadian per barrel on Hibernia because I think that is what it will cost to get out of there-what will happen is that taxpayers will be left with a $2.7 billion plus debt.
You are sounding like the Tories.

The member said I am sounding like the Tories. I am just sound fiscally responsible. We are in Ontario, you know.

I tell them, before they clap, to remember that this enterprise is Canadian. This makes it a guarantee of Canadian sources. We in the NDP want Canadian sources. We want Canadian control of Hibernia. We do not want a government, in false promises to people, guaranteeing jobs that will not be there or guaranteeing a project that is not going to benefit all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak in this debate this afternoon. I had intended to speak briefly.

Through the development of what initially was discussions about the imposition of regulations by the Newfoundland government, there have been huge changes as the project has changed, as the science has changed, as the corporate world has changed, as the political world has changed. battles over control of the resource and whose responsibility this would be and who would pay for that.
We saw the Atlantic Accord. We have seen the signing of principles. At the beginning of this month we saw the signing to start the project, but as I sit here and listen to this debate and listen to my good friend from Gander-Grand Falls and my friend from British Columbia, I think of all the things we would like to have.
Yes, we would like to see this project proceed with no subsidies. We would love to see this project proceed, developed by just Canadian companies, and all the work done just in Canadian shipyards or with Canadian products. We would love to see no giveaways for Newfoundland- everything Newfoundland wants it gets, and everything Quebec and Ontario and New Brunswick want they get. That would be great, except there is only one problem: there would be no project.
That is not true.

Mobil Oil.

Then, we are

talking about a series of six or seven other projects that are ready to go, Wild Rose, Ben Nevis and numerous others. We are not just talking about cement and steel and putting steel together and putting it on a big platform. We are talking about engineering.

Well, now it is our chance to build our own home where people can live and work in the place where they grew up and want to live. They will build their futures for their kids.

the new kids phraseology, it is the new heads on the block.

-waiting for the guillotine.

Government Orders
that all four of these men went into this exercise with their hands tied behind their backs because, you see, they had to negotiate a deal within the parameters of the 1988 Statement of Principles.

Will he tell us in at least some general terms what kinds of safeguards there are because this is an industry that is going to be with us for 20, 30 or 40 years.
We have an industry that has been with us for 500 years. I have in my riding alone 17,000 people, men and women, who make their living either in the boats or in the fish plants throughout the riding of Burin-St. George's, 17,000.
They are just part of the total number throughout Newfoundland and Labrador, so it would be a disaster not only in economic terms but in cultural and way-of-life terms too. This would be an unmitigated disaster. I want to have on the public record some of the preventive steps that are being taken and some of the compensation, if you can ever compensate should the unthinkable happen. I want to hear in some detail from the minister what the ministry and the government have in mind should all not go as well as one would like.
There is another issue here that I want to raise. I am covering several subjects quickly because I am not going to be in the Chamber tomorrow. I will be in my riding. I am not sure when the bill might get through. If it is around next week, I have some other things I want to say. I want to get one of those in the record. I hope we have not tied our hands behind our backs in another respect. I hope in getting a labour piece agreement for this project, and that in itself was a commendable effort, I hope we have not short-changed the opportunities for people with skills who are close to the project in terms of where they live but who happen not to have a particular union card. That is going to be a very difficult, frustrating issue if there are people whose only sin is that they do not belong to a particular union.

An important issue that spins off from that is what happened to the union at the Marystown shipyard. As a result of a decision on jurisdiction that went against them in the period leading up to the culmination of the agreement, there will be a situation for people in my riding and the town of Marystown.
The Marystown shipyard will fabricate certain items for the project. At some point in time, as is often the case with these large items that have to be built at one site and then transported to another site for integration of the over-all project, they will have a situation where all the work will not be able to be done at the Marystown shipyard. It will be desirable to do some at the GBS site, in this case at Great Mosquito Cove.
They have been told, as the minister will probably be aware, that any work they do on that item that they will have contracted must be done at Marystown, and once it moves to the other site they have no participation in the finish of that particular work.
That, in my view, is an absolutely mad scheme. I see my time is up so I will clue up for now. On behalf of the people who are directly affected, the workers at the Marystown shipyard, at Cowhead in particular, I make a plea. If there is a way to moderate that in some particular fashion, I would appeal to him to use his best efforts to do so. I may come back to that later if there is a further opportunity, but I realize my time is up.
